newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's army gears up for thrust against rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's army gears up for thrust against rebels.

text.p: Zaire's army is gearing up for a promised counter-offensive against the Tutsi-led rebels in the east who humiliated it in 1996.
Three Russian-built combat helicopters, bristling with rockets and 24 mm cannon, circle over the eastern town of Kisangani, the likely springboard for the attack.
"It won't be long before this adventure is over," the governor of Upper Zaire, Lombeya Bosongo, told Reuters. He would not elaborate.
Military officers in Zaire's fourth largest town say little about preparations, nothing about the timing of the thrust.
But soldiers drive around this crumbling regional capital in the heart of Zaire's equatorial rainforest in new vehicles.
Sometimes foreign mercenaries accompany them. One senior dignitary in the region put the number of mercenaries at 300.
Witnesses report regular arrivals of planes in recent days and weeks with weapons and men.
Boxes of ammunition line the tarmac. Soldiers carrying heavy back-packs file out of unmarked planes. A Puma helicopter awaits deployment.
Senior army officers describe the airport, 17 km (10 miles) from town, as the military headquarters for the counter-attack.
Army chief of staff General Mahele Leiko Bokoungo, appointed in December with wide-ranging powers, arrived last week.
The rebels, who launched their offensive in October, hold the towns of Goma, Bukavu, Bunia and Uvira as well as territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.
The central government in Kinshasa accuses Rwanda, where Tutsis wrested the upperhand from Hutus after the 1994 Rwandan genocide, of fighting alongside the rebels.
For over a month, the government has been promising a counter-attack.

Veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko returned home in December after cancer surgery and four months rest in Europe and reshuffled the government and army leadership to confront the rebels. He has since returned to Europe for more medical tests.
Dismissing talk of negotiating while towns and territory are occupied, the government has thrown its weight behind the military option.
Zairean intelligence and other sources say the army has launched numerous small-scale operations into rebel territory.
The rebels say they have rebuffed these advances inflicting serious casualties on the army.
They have even talked of taking Kisangani, which is on the banks of the mighty Zaire River.
As part of Mahele's efforts to restore discipline in Zaire's rag-tag army, 15 soldiers, including senior officers, will stand trial on Tuesday on charges ranging from desertion to pillage.
A special military tribunal would hear the case, a senior military magistrate told Reuters.

Residents of Kisangani have mixed feelings about the presence of the army. They have bitter memories of recent looting by poorly paid soldiers and operations against rebels by Zairean soldiers and mercenaries in the 1960s.
"They should pay and equip the Zairean army instead of buying in foreigners to fight," one taxi driver commented.
